tagline: Roads to the springs connect Washington family homes and canal engineering.
intro: The Washington Heritage Trail loops through West Virginia’s Eastern Panhandle on county roads and state and U.S. highways, with a western spur to Paw Paw. Its own guide describes 136 miles linking eighteenth-century towns, industrial sites, Washington family homes, springs and mountain ranges. At Panorama Overlook, the view takes in the Potomac and Cacapon rivers, the C&O Canal and the B&O Railroad.

Travel to the springs helped shape an earlier road across this country. In 1832, builder Silas Harry erected the Van Metre Ford Stone Bridge over Opequon Creek, improving the Warm Springs Road between Alexandria and Bath. The modern heritage circuit received state byway designation in 1998 and national designation in 2000. It brings Washington family sites together with museums, historic districts and parks. The byway’s name reflects George Washington’s connections to the region, but the trail also takes in later industrial sites, including a canal tunnel begun in 1836.

Start at Paw Paw, with the canal tunnel excursion across the Potomac in Maryland, then travel east on WV 9 to Berkeley Springs. The southern branch heads toward Charles Town and Harpers Ferry. From Harpers Ferry, the northern branch returns toward Berkeley Springs on WV 230, WV 480 and WV 9.

moments.title: Paw Paw Tunnel
moments.text: More than six million bricks line Paw Paw Tunnel, a 3,118-foot passage built to bypass bends in the Potomac. The C&O Canal Company began construction in 1836, expecting the work to take two years. Engineering and financial problems stopped work from 1841 to 1847. The tunnel opened in 1850, and canal boats continued using it until 1924. A semaphore signal was installed at the west end in 1872 to control boat traffic. Across the river from Paw Paw in Maryland, the surviving towpath leads into the tunnel. The passage was so narrow that nobody could pass between the mules and the tunnel wall.
moments.notice: The brick lining follows the canal passage through the ridge.

moments.title: George Washington's Bathtub, Berkeley Springs
moments.text: A spring bubbles through the stone tub on the west side of Berkeley Springs State Park. The tub is a reconstruction from the 1930s, representing early bathing conditions. The trail’s guide describes the earlier arrangement as scooped-out pools lined with sand and rocks, screened by woven brush. Washington first visited the springs in 1748, aged sixteen, and wrote of repeated visits. In a 1761 letter, he described visitors whose complaints improved in the water and others who found no relief. The springs also supply the town’s tap water. Five major springs merge at the spa.
moments.notice: A spring bubbles up through the reconstructed stone tub.

moments.title: Jefferson Rock, Harpers Ferry
moments.text: Jefferson Rock is a stack of Harpers shale above the meeting of the Shenandoah and Potomac. Thomas Jefferson stood here on October 25, 1783, and praised the view in Notes on the State of Virginia. Four stone pillars were later placed beneath the upper slab after its natural support deteriorated. The approach climbs old stone steps above St. Peter’s Church. From the formation, the river confluence and the gap through the Blue Ridge share the view with a railroad tunnel mouth and the restored town. The formation is within Harpers Ferry National Historical Park, reached along the Appalachian Trail.
moments.notice: Four stone pillars support the upper slab of Harpers shale.
